questions.knowledge_point: Understanding the Even Extension of a Function
questions.worked_solution:
If $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in [0,\pi ),$ the even extension of $F$ is the function $f$ such that

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}F(x), & x\in [0,\pi ), \\ F(-x), & x\in (-\pi ,0).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, for $x\in (-\pi ,0),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =F(-x) \\  & =(-x)^{2}+2(-x)+3 \\  & ={x}^{2}-2x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-3) & =(-3)^{2}-2(-3)+3=18.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)
$$

Let $F(x)=3{x}^{2}+2$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ The Fourier cosine series of the **even** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the expression for ${a}_{0}.$

${a}_{0}=$ {{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
For our Fourier cosine series, the constant term is given by

$$
{a}_{0}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=3{x}^{2}+2$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(3{x}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }{[{x}^{3}+2x]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }({\pi }^{3}+2\pi )-0 \\  & =2({\pi }^{2}+2).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Cosine Coefficients From the Half-Range Formula
questions.problem:
Let $F(x)=-2x+5$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ Select the correct missing parts in the Fourier cosine series of the **even** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of the function $F(x)$ below.

$$
f(x)∼(5-\pi )+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot {{field-2}}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=-2x+5$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(-2x+5)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=-2x+5\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=-2 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{2}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }(\frac{1}{n}[(-2x+5)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{2}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{n\pi }(((-2\pi +5)\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-5\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))-\frac{2}{n}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =\frac{2}{n\pi }(0-\frac{2}{n}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{4(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi ))}{{n}^{2}\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{4(1-(-1)^{n})}{\pi {n}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, the Fourier cosine series is

$$
f(x)∼(5-\pi )+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{4(1-(-1)^{n})}{\pi {n}^{2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(nx).
$$

In our case, $f(x)=-6x-2$ for $x \in (0,\pi).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
a_n = \dfrac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi (-6x-2) \cos(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=-6x-2\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=-6 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{2}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }(\frac{1}{n}[(-6x-2)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{6}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{n\pi }(((-6\pi -2)\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))-\frac{6}{n}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =\frac{2}{n\pi }(0-\frac{6}{n}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{12(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi ))}{{n}^{2}\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $\cos(n\pi)=(-1)^n,$ we have

$$
a_n = \dfrac{12(1-(-1)^n)}{\pi n^2}.
$$

Finally, the Fourier cosine series is

$$
f(x) \sim (-2-3\pi) + \sum_{n=1}^\infty 
\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{12(1-(-1)^n)}{\pi n^2}} 
\cdot 
\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\cos(nx)}.
$$
